seoTitle: Discounted cash flow Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Discounted cash flow: work out earnings per share from the first FCFF and the second FCFF. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: Give the Discounted cash flow calculator the first FCFF, the second FCFF, the third FCFF and the fourth FCFF and it returns earnings per share. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Discounted cash flow calculator work?
sections.html:
The Discounted cash flow calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports earnings per share in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the DCF method); then you type in the first FCFF, the second FCFF, the third FCFF and the fourth FCFF.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Discounted cash flow calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Earnings per share=growth value × (-discount rate + growth rate) ÷ (growth rate × ((growth rate + 1) ÷ (discount rate + 1), over the next...) − growth rate + ((growth rate + 1) ÷ (discount rate + 1), over the next...) − 1)
Terminal value=earnings per share × ((growth rate + 1) ÷ (discount rate + 1), over the next...) × (-terminal growth rate × ((terminal growth rate + 1) ÷ (discount rate + 1), over the next...) + terminal growth rate − ((terminal growth rate + 1) ÷ (discount rate + 1), over the next...) + 1) ÷ (discount rate − terminal growth rate)
Terminal value=total intrinsic value − growth value

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Discounted cash flow calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the first FCFF, the second FCFF and the third FCFF — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Discounted cash flow calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns earnings per share, derived from the first FCFF, the second FCFF and the third FCFF. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Discounted cash flow calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the first FCFF, the second FCFF, the third FCFF and the fourth FCFF, which is 28 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter first FCFF in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. First FCFF opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (9 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Discounted cash flow calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
